When using an HTML document/table, even just including one more line of code significantly improves the formatting. There are 6 additional alternative HTML table theme options apart from the default bootstrap theme: 

* `kable_styling()` for the bootstrap theme 
1. `kable_classic()`
2. `kable_classic2()`
3. `kable_paper()`
4. `kable_minimal()`
5. `kable_material()`
6. `kable_material_dark()`


::: {.callout-important}
The majority of `{kableExtra}` functions will work in [both HTML and PDF rendered files](https://github.com/haozhu233/kableExtra#basic-usage). When using a PDF file, you need to use the argument `latex_options` instead as you are producing LaTeX tables. When using `{kableExtra}` functions, it is recommended by the package authors to use the wrapper function `kbl()` instead of `kable()`. Pull up the documentation of `kbl()` with the using the `?` function to learn more. 
:::

## Top tip - document and chunk outlines 

Once your Quarto document starts to get quite long (you've been working hard!), with several different headings and perhaps various subheadings too, it can start to get slightly tricky to quickly scroll and find the various sections in your raw document.

To help with this, RStudio have a helpful tool, the **Show document outline** (which is the button with various lines stacked on top of each other) option which you can find near the **Run** menu. This will show you an interactive outline of your document by the different headers/sections you have created. 

This lets you quickly jump between sections in your document and see the outline of your structure at a glance. A similar interactive outline feature can be found at the bottom of your document/source pane, and code chunks are included here too.

# Functionalities of different output formats 

In Quarto, HTML and PDF files are the richest formats for document rendering. In general, when rendering to an `html` there are more interesting functionalities. Indeed, Markdown was originally designed for HTML output so the HTML format has the richest features. 

There are some features that you can add to your YAML document options that are shared across both HTML and PDF outputs; these should be specified at **root level**. Root level means that the option applies to all formats (e.g. where `title` and `author` go, before the `format` options are specified). The `format` option is where we provide format-specific options (aptly named). 

These include:

* table of contents
* syntax-highlighting 
* section numbering 

## HTML 

You can have a look at some of the options when rendering to HTML in the [Quarto documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/reference/formats/html.html). 

::: {.callout-tip}
## Where to start with HTML documentation 
 
As a suggested starting point, look at the options around **table of contents**, **numbering**, and **code**. 
:::

There are also HTML specific code block options, which [you can review here](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-code.html). Pay particular attention to **folding code** and **code tools** for some really cool interactive options.

## PDF 

PDFs in Quarto also have a variety of features. To find out more, check out the [Quarto documentation around PDF format options](https://quarto.org/docs/reference/formats/pdf.html) 

## Themes 

In general, there are a [variety of theme options available](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html) to use with Quarto HTML documents. More advanced use cases around themeing involve custom CSS files, **which we will not be covering and is not permitted in this course**. Quarto includes 25 themes from the Bootswatch project built in - no further customisation needed. These range from light to dark themes.

# Reproducibility! 

In practice, depending on your audience, you will need to decide to show your code or not. It is unlikely that you will want to show the code used to produce your analysis, tables, or figures to an audience unfamiliar with R and would therefore set `echo: false` in the set-up chunk. For this course, though, and in particular for the datathon report, you will need to set `echo: true` so that we can see your code and the product of that code. 

While it can take up space, it is good practice to finish a document calling the `sessionInfo()` function, which lists all of the packages you used, their versions, and more. 

```{r}
#| label: session-info
#| echo: false

sessionInfo()

```
